I’ve been following this discussion with much interest, and wanted to provide a mathematical interpretation to you of @chirogonemd‘s points, as I understand them. I believe what he is saying is logically sound.

First, let’s clarify some assumptions: I think we can all agree that the universal domain of scientific, philosophical, and other intellectual knowledge and invention is far too great for any single human to fully explore to maximum depth AND breadth. Thus, each individual will end up choosing a subset of all knowledge (and invention) to focus on. The key here is that we’re establishing the notion of a “finite intellectual budget”, which is insufficient to afford the “purchase” of all possible intellectual pursuits.

Now, suppose we have two individuals with the same intellectual budget: person A and person B. Supposing person A chose a very different subset than person B (on which to spend their finite intellectual budget), they will unlikely be able to communicate or collaborate deeply and meaningfully on most subjects they find interesting — particularly those of the greatest “depth” and specialty (if we visualize a taxonomy of knowledge as a fuzzy tree, with core principles of logic and rationality near the root).

Now suppose instead that persons A and B have exactly the same knowledge and intellectual budget at some time T. As time progresses, suppose A and B pursue slightly different avenues of research and invention, and this continues for a very long time. Inevitably, after long enough, A and B’s set of knowledge and inventions will diverge until mutual understanding is again not productive, without considerable effort of each side to familiarize with the other’s innovations.

This demonstrates that lack of mutually productive understanding in deep intellectual specialties is at least not entirely a symptom of mismatched intelligence, but of domain specific knowledge — whether the divergence is learned and/or individually invented.

The degree to which specialty knowledge vs pure intelligence plays a role here then depends on how nonlinear the relationship is between one’s IQ and the “depth cost” of nodes in the knowledge graph model I mentioned above: if the relative cost of nodes vary as a function of depth and intelligence, then indeed intelligence could become the dominating factor here. So really, the question is what this function looks like.

For example, perhaps we experience exponentially increasing difficulty in learning deeper and deeper subjects, where IQ is actually modifying the base of that exponent (rather than a linear multiplier) with other factors perhaps also adding in a linear bias and gain. In this model of intelligence, it would be possible for people with a higher IQ to be fundamentally capable of orders of magnitude more depth, while simultaneously less capable of breadth at shallower levels of the knowledge tree!

I think it is clearly the case that this function is nonlinear, but it’s an open question as to exactly what the shape of this function is. There are at least a few studies showing that above 120-130, most barriers go away and other factors like hard work and specialization play a far greater role towards success. But at the same time, I think it’s quite clear that someone with an IQ of 70-80 will never be capable of understanding, let alone innovating, in particularly deep fields (say, theoretical physics, abstract mathematics, computer science, etc.) It is therefore at least plausible that someone with an IQ or 190 may be able to understand and formulate concepts even someone with an IQ of 150 might never even begin to comprehend, no matter the effort.

With that said, based on the studies I have seen, I am skeptical of this. It seems there are diminishing returns for extremely high IQs. It is also possible that these diminishing returns represent a flaw in our ability to measure general intelligence behind a few standard deviations from the mean (remember: IQ is an approximation that works extremely well over large groups; but when we start pushing enough stddev’s from the mean, your data becomes a sparse set of outliers).
